entities.name: Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, established in 1977 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, emerged as a pivotal human rights organization during the country's Dirty War, a period marked by state terrorism against dissidents. Comprised primarily of elderly women whose children were forcibly disappeared by the military dictatorship, this group became a symbol of resilience and resistance against oppression, advocating for truth and justice in a tumultuous political landscape. Their headquarters, located in the iconic Plaza de Mayo, served as a focal point for public demonstrations and a site of solidarity for families seeking answers about their missing loved ones.

Through tireless protests and the iconic act of wearing white headscarves symbolizing their lost grandchildren, the Grandmothers garnered national and international attention, leading to the establishment of legal proceedings against former military officials. They played a crucial role in the formation of the Argentine truth commission and were instrumental in the development of policies aimed at addressing impunity, ultimately uncovering the fates of thousands of desaparecidos (the disappeared). Their efforts culminated in the identification of over 130 grandchildren who were illegally adopted during the dictatorship, reintegrating them with their biological families.
